metadata.title: Thinking Skills in Teaching Practices: Relationship with Students’ Achievement in Mathematics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study links teacher-reported mathematics teaching practices to students’ mathematics achievement using TIMSS and PISA scores, with analyses clustered at the data level. The methodology states that regression residuals were corrected using Huber–White robust standard errors because the data were clustered, but it does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. No specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is named, so the paper’s weighting strategy for population-representative inference cannot be confirmed from the provided text. The analytic sample is restricted by the teacher questionnaire items: three teaching-practice response lines (c, g, k) were excluded because no response distribution was obtained, and the models include control variables at student, class, teacher, and school levels.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are TIMSS and PISA mathematics scores used in SEM/regression-style models, but the paper does not describe whether these scores are PV-based achievement estimates, WLE/theta scores, or how PVs were handled if applicable. Because the manuscript text provided does not document any missing-data procedure (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) for the analytic sample, the missing-data handling is a reporting gap. This limits reproducibility and may affect effect sizes if missingness is non-trivial and not handled consistently.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses teacher questionnaire responses on eleven mathematics teaching practices, but excludes three response lines (c, g, and k) because no response distribution was obtained for them. Teaching practices are grouped into lower-order (LO) and higher-order (HO) factors using confirmatory factor analysis, and SEM/regression models are estimated with control variables including students’ socioeconomic status (mother’s education and books at home) and aggregated class/school characteristics (e.g., class size, % female, average socioeconomic status), plus teacher and school characteristics. The paper reports N of observations for the regression/SEM models (3,414 for teacher/class characteristics models; 3,394–3,413 for TIMSS/PISA score models), but does not specify country coverage or grade-level country-level sample sizes in the provided text.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression/SEM coefficients (Table 4, Models 1–3): LO practices: 0.01 (not significant) in Model 1; HO practices: 0.70*** (Model 2) and 0.78*** (Model 3). Controls: Books at home 0.15***; Mother’s education 0.11***. N of observations: 3,394–3,413 depending on model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS (mathematics, eighth grade) the study leveraged higher-order teaching practices (HO) and lower-order teaching practices (LO), together with books at home and mother’s education, to explain mathematics achievement, finding that HO practices had a strong positive association with TIMSS scores (about +0.70 to +0.78 SD per 1 SD increase), while LO practices showed no significant relationship. This indicates that classroom instruction emphasizing higher-order thinking tasks is more strongly linked to students’ mathematics performance than routine/lower-order practice, suggesting policy should prioritize cognitive-activation teaching practices in math.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression/SEM coefficients (Table 4, Models 4–6): HO practices: 0.71*** (Model 4) and 0.75*** (Model 6). LO practices: initially positive 0.11*** (Model 4) but becomes negative when HO is controlled for: −0.16*** (Model 6). Controls: Books at home 0.17***; Mother’s education 0.10***. N of observations: 3,394–3,413 depending on model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA (mathematics, ninth grade) the study leveraged higher-order teaching practices (HO) and lower-order teaching practices (LO), together with books at home and mother’s education, to explain mathematics achievement, finding that HO practices were consistently positively associated with PISA scores (about +0.71 to +0.75 SD per 1 SD increase) while the LO association reversed direction once HO was included (LO became significantly negative at −0.16 SD). This indicates that emphasizing higher-order thinking in math instruction may be a more effective lever for improving achievement than relying on lower-order, routine-focused practices, and that LO effects may reflect substitution with HO rather than independent benefit.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA (mathematics, ninth grade) controlling for TIMSS performance
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (PISA scores) net of TIMSS
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 5 (Models 7–9): LO practices: 0.10*** (Model 7) but −0.01 (Model 8) and insignificant trend when TIMSS is controlled (Model 8–9). HO practices: 0.32*** (Model 7) and 0.31*** (Model 9). TIMSS scores in mathematics: 0.59*** to 0.56***. Controls: Books at home 0.08*** to 0.09***; Mother’s education 0.03* to 0.04*. N of observations: 3,394–3,357 depending on model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA (mathematics, ninth grade) data with TIMSS mathematics scores controlled, the study leveraged higher-order teaching practices (HO), lower-order teaching practices (LO), and prior achievement (TIMSS scores), finding that HO practices retained a positive association with PISA performance (about +0.31 to +0.32 SD per 1 SD increase) while LO practices lost significance once prior achievement was accounted for. This indicates that higher-order thinking-oriented instruction is linked to achievement gains beyond baseline performance, supporting education policy that targets cognitive-activation teaching practices rather than only routine skill repetition.

data.outcome_summary: The study examines how teacher-reported mathematics teaching practices relate to students’ mathematics achievement in the eighth grade (TIMSS) and ninth grade (PISA), using SEM/confirmatory factor analysis to construct lower-order (LO) and higher-order (HO) teaching practice scales. It reports that HO practices show a strong positive association with TIMSS scores (coefficients around 0.70–0.78 SD) and with PISA scores (around 0.71–0.75 SD), while LO practices are not significant in TIMSS and become negative in PISA when HO is included. When PISA is modeled while controlling for TIMSS performance, HO remains significant (about 0.31–0.32 SD), whereas LO loses significance, suggesting effects persist beyond prior achievement. The paper uses Huber–White robust standard errors for clustered data but does not report PV handling or a missing-data strategy in the provided text, limiting interpretability and reproducibility.
